## Learning objectives

By the end of this opening, you should be able to state the research question, identify the unit represented by a row of data, describe what another researcher would need to retrace a result, and explain how Git and GitHub record, review, and share changes.

You will read the workshop's Git history yourself, then watch the environment, metadata, versioning, and archiving demonstrations. In the hands-on segment you will complete and run the pipeline and revise its report. If you arrive late, finish [preparation](00_preparation.qmd) during the demonstrations.

## Why this matters

A reported result is easier to evaluate when its data, analytical decisions, code, and software environment can be traced. Sharing code helps, but the code also needs identifiable inputs and instructions that work beyond its author's current R session.

In this workshop, **reproducibility** means being able to rerun a documented workflow with its specified inputs and environment. **Open science** also concerns how methods and outputs can be inspected, accessed, and reused. Throughout the session, ask whether another researcher could understand, rerun, audit, trace, reuse, and cite the work. 

## Our example: health and well-being

**What association between health and well-being is reported across the included studies?** We use the `HealthWellbeing` correlation example [@harrer2021, sec. 4.2.4].

Each row is a **study summary**. The columns are:

| Column       | Meaning                       |
|--------------|-------------------------------|
| `author`     | Study label                   |
| `cor`        | Reported Pearson correlation  |
| `n`          | Study sample size             |
| `population` | Sample population description |
| `country`    | Study country                 |

## One workflow throughout the session

We follow this dataset through one connected workflow. The first half opens with a short Git activity; in the second half, you complete, run, and change the analysis yourself to understand and experience the whole workflow.

## Version control with Git and GitHub {#git-github}

**Git** records the history of a project's files. **GitHub** hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration tools such as issues, pull requests, and releases.

| Term | Meaning |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Commit | A recorded change to one or more files, with a message explaining why |
| Branch | A line of work that can change without affecting the main version |
| Remote | A copy of the repository elsewhere, such as on GitHub |
| Push | Send local commits to a remote repository |
| Pull request | A proposal to merge a branch, with a place for review and discussion |
| Release | A named, tagged version of the repository, covered later in the session |

### Read the workshop's history {#git-history}

The project in your MyBinder session is a copy of the files without their Git history, but Git can read the history of the public repository directly.

1. **Which versions have been released?** List the repository's tags without downloading anything else.

```{bash git-versions, include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, cache = FALSE, output = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
url=https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r.git
git ls-remote --tags --refs "$url"
```

Each line pairs a commit hash with a version tag. A tag gives one commit a permanent name. We will later cover how Zenodo archives each tagged release with its own DOI.

2. **What changed recently, and why?** Copy the history into a temporary folder. `--filter=blob:none` fetches the commits and the lists of files they changed, but not the file contents, so it takes a few seconds.

```{bash git-clone, include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, cache = FALSE, output = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
rm -rf /tmp/workshop-history.git
url=https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r.git
git clone --quiet --bare --filter=blob:none "$url" /tmp/workshop-history.git
git -C /tmp/workshop-history.git log --oneline --no-merges -5
git -C /tmp/workshop-history.git log --oneline -3 -- pipelines/_targets_health_wellbeing.R
```

The first log lists the latest changes, and each message says what
changed. The second lists only the commits that changed the
reference pipeline.

3. **Is the reference pipeline in your session the latest version?** Git identifies each version of a file by a hash of its contents. Compare the copy in your MyBinder project with the one in the latest commit.

```{bash git-hash, include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, cache = FALSE, output = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
git hash-object pipelines/_targets_health_wellbeing.R
git -C /tmp/workshop-history.git rev-parse HEAD:pipelines/_targets_health_wellbeing.R
```

Matching lines mean identical contents. If they differ, the repository changed after your MyBinder environment was built. This is why a result should cite a specific commit or release rather than "the latest version". 

## Discuss with a neighbour

Name one thing you would ask for if a collaborator sent you a meta-analysis manuscript for the `HealthWellbeing` dataset. Choose from the data version, variable definitions, analysis settings, code revision, or software environment, and explain why it would matter.

Allow about one minute.
